CRM for a property agency: ready-made or custom development

When a ready-made CRM is enough, when specialist software helps and when custom development makes sense. Features, prices and implementation at Shepit House and Delmar.

An agency needing to record enquiries and move clients through sales stages can start with an off-the-shelf CRM such as Kommo. If property data, client selections and listing publication drive the work, a specialist platform such as RealtSoft deserves consideration. Custom development makes sense for particular workflows, interfaces or combinations of features that are hard to assemble in an existing product. RESET compares launch and ongoing costs against the agency's work. Here we use Kommo for Shepit House and our Estate CRM for Delmar as examples.

01

When an agency needs a CRM

The need becomes clear when enquiries come from several sources and clients move between employees. One agent answers, another conducts a viewing, and a manager agrees special terms, but no shared history exists. Clients repeat their requirements while staff reconstruct agreements from messages. Even a simple record with an owner and next action can help. An agency with two people and a steady enquiry flow should consider it.

Headcount is only a guide. Two people using several advertising channels may need automatic deals and tasks. Five people handling a few referrals may only need a pipeline and reminders. Assess enquiry volume, deal duration, handovers and manual work. Holidays or departures expose the problem: if client history leaves with the agent, shared records are already necessary.

02

What a property CRM should do

The foundation connects client, property, deal and next action. Agents need requirements, suitable listings, previous conversation outcomes and follow-up dates. Managers need stages, sources and stalled deals. Office staff may need to maintain listing details, photographs and prices. Connected data reduces searching and repeated entry.

A CRM also reveals what happens after advertising generates an enquiry. Without later statuses, marketers cannot easily distinguish suitable buyers from accidental requests or duplicates. Consistent qualification and progression enable quality comparisons. Suitable integrations can send CRM events to advertising platforms in line with technical and data requirements. Connecting a CRM does not guarantee lower lead costs; event quality, data volume and campaign setup matter. See property advertising on Facebook and Instagram.

03

Comparing Kommo, RealtSoft and a custom CRM

General-purpose, specialist and custom systems overlap but require different implementation. A general CRM adapts pipelines, fields and integrations. A property platform already includes familiar concepts. Custom development begins with agreed logic and features. Test each using one real journey: receive an enquiry, match properties, send options and schedule follow-up.

Three approaches to property CRM
CriterionKommoRealtSoftCustom CRM

04

When Kommo fits

Consider Kommo for inbound enquiries, messages, ownership and sales stages. A small team can organise work without commissioning a separate product. Setup includes pipelines, fields and chosen sources. Check automation and integrations against the plan and requirements. A full property catalogue needs a separate assessment of the data model and selection tools.

For Shepit House, we chose two Kommo seats to organise leads and make follow-up transparent. The team needed to know what happened after an ad enquiry and who owned the next step. Setup and implementation took two weeks. The CRM formed part of lead generation, connecting incoming demand with processing. See the Shepit House case study; assess CRM's contribution alongside advertising and sales work.

05

When a specialist property CRM is useful

Specialist software helps agents handle many properties and regularly send selections. RealtSoft's website describes its property database, presentations, offer-sharing and telephony connections. Check whether these workflows fit daily work. A good fit reduces custom setup. Follow an entire client journey in a demonstration and inspect what buyers receive.

Discuss interface changes, exports and service connections separately. A platform follows a shared roadmap, so special requirements may need vendor agreement, such as a different selection format or property workflow. A large feature library matters only if staff use it. We assess the number of daily steps and how much of the interface would be unnecessary.

06

Why Delmar chose Estate CRM

Delmar's nine-person team wanted a particular combination: property data, deal management, reminders and its own way of sending selections. A clear interface focused on daily functions was important. Specialist platforms also offer selections; the decision concerned the preferred workflow and control over the product. We designed Estate CRM around these requirements and limited the first version to agreed tasks.

The system includes a catalogue, a deal kanban and Telegram task notifications, reaching employees in a familiar channel. It also connects to VIA, our Telegram Mini App for preparing and sending property selections. Together these features form a continuous client-and-property workflow. See the Delmar Estate CRM case study.

The first version took a month and a half to develop and implement, with a $1500 budget and one month of agreed support. This price refers to Delmar's specific initial scope. Extensions, new integrations and logic changes require separate estimates. Comparisons with ready-made products must include future development and infrastructure.

07

CRM implementation costs

RESET's basic configuration of an existing CRM starts at $250, while a typical client implementation is around $500. Complex integrations, automation and migration can raise this to $800-1000 or more. Custom development starts at $1500 after defining the initial version. Cost depends on workflows, source-data condition, connections and staff requirements. Platform licences and paid external services are separate.

We separate client records, catalogue, integrations, notifications and migration in the estimate. Clients can distinguish launch requirements from later additions. An agency might begin with deals and listings, then connect property portals after validating the main process. This aligns budget with current work. See development costs with AI for scope and new tools.

08

Subscription or custom CRM: which costs less?

Compare at least a year using equivalent requirements. A ready-made CRM involves setup, licences, paid integrations and support. A custom one involves development, hosting, services, maintenance and new features. Avoiding per-seat charges can benefit a growing team, but somebody must own updates, backups and fixes.

As an illustration, a $25 monthly licence for nine users costs $225 a month or $2700 a year before discounts and extras. This is arithmetic, not a current tariff: check Kommo pricing for region, billing period and plan. A $1500 first version plus hypothetical infrastructure at $20 a month totals $1740 in year one before support, paid integrations and changes. Compare functionality before claiming savings.

We estimate that modest custom CRM infrastructure under moderate load can fit within $20 a month. Growing databases, images and data exchange can increase this to $100 or more. Paid telephony, messages and other services add costs where needed. Specialist maintenance and development are also separate. We document recurring costs and included support so clients understand the post-launch budget.

09

How RESET implements a CRM

We review sources, staff roles, stages and property records. Reconstruct several real client journeys from first message to viewing or rejection. This reveals lost enquiries, repeated actions and manual transfers. Then define essential initial features and integrations, producing a clear description of what the system does for each role.

We compare ready-made products and assess custom development where justified. For existing software, agree settings, connections and migration. For a bespoke system, prepare a specification and key-screen prototype to verify workflows before coding. Test real scenarios: stored enquiries, assigned owners and delivered notifications. Launch includes explaining daily actions to staff and an agreed support period.

10

Why employees stop updating the CRM

A system that demands reporting but provides little daily help is often the problem. Agents re-enter messages, fill unclear fields and use stages that do not reflect real deals. Work drifts back to private notes and messengers. Walk through everyday tasks with staff to find unnecessary steps. Fields, automation and alerts need an understandable purpose.

Start with the minimum needed to continue: contact, requirements, owner, current stage and next action. Use reveals which details help sales and which reports managers need. Agree who updates deals, creates tasks and hands clients over. Even a well-chosen CRM requires those rules; a usable interface helps people follow them.

11

Choosing for your agency

For enquiries and deals, begin by checking a general-purpose CRM. For properties, selections and publication, include a specialist product. For specific interaction, logic and feature control, assess custom development. In every case, request a complete journey using your client example and calculate ongoing costs. RESET can review this with your team and propose a scope suited to your current scale.

12

Sources and basis of comparison

This comparison draws on RESET implementations and vendor-published capabilities. Shepit House and Delmar timings and prices refer to their agreed scopes. RESET figures are in US dollars; annual examples need adjustment for your team. Before commissioning, we check current plans, tariffs and external service terms. Official product pages follow.
